docs.title: Reference-aware retention (#60)
docs.text:
Historical component delivery record. Normal worker/UI integration now requires individual exact-proposal confirmation; see the #62 report.

The advanced incremental executor supports opt-in cleanup. The normal worker is still not switched to v4. All operations use the approved manual-offline, single-owning-computer model, the shared state directory's non-expiring set UUID lock, and fresh owner/epoch checks. This is not remote fencing.

docs.title: Use and authorization
docs.text:
Set retention to a positive newest-N count in the incremental JSON request. Omit it (or use zero through the C++ API) to disable automatic cleanup planning. Optionally set legacy_root to the exact old legacy set folder. It must be separate from the shared repository; no recursive search or hostname guessing is used. Legacy copies and snapshots share one creation-time/identity ordering. Incomplete legacy states remain intact and consume no successful-history slot. Unreadable, unsupported or ambiguous history blocks cleanup rather than being ignored.

An optional historical Proton folder that is absent contributes no copies, even if one of its ancestors is also absent. Absence must be established from a complete, name/UID/parent-validated ancestor listing; download errors, unreadable listings, UID aliases and identity mismatches are never treated as absence. Required repository inventories and exact deletion targets retain their strict checks.

Only a verified, durably completed saved publication can start a proposal. Unchanged checks publish no snapshot and consume no slot. Failed uploads, quota errors, and incomplete backups cannot start retention. No history is removed to make upload space.

The saved result includes cleanup_proposal, its cleanup_confirmation SHA-256, and cleanup_needs_attention. Review the entire proposal before copying that hash into the request's cleanup_confirmation. Then run:

build/omacustos-incremental --request request.json \
  --acknowledge-single-writer --cleanup

--cleanup plans/retries cleanup without rerunning the writer. A fresh scope needs a fresh confirmation; this implementation deliberately requires exact confirmation for every proposal rather than granting an open-ended deletion policy. Once authorization is persisted, retry needs no new confirmation for the same bytes. Never pass a proposal from another set/root/owner. A pending proposal blocks all writers, even before confirmation; finish/reconcile it before continuing backups. Offline takeover refuses unfinished cleanup. Completed proposals survive handoff as validated historical records, not reusable deletion authority.

Backup success is independent of cleanup success. If cleanup fails, the executor keeps the saved snapshot and reports Backup saved; cleanup needs attention. Do not retry by starting a different writer operation; use --cleanup with the original saved request. No cloud commands were run during automated validation.

docs.title: Safety and durable ordering
docs.text:
1. Freshly validate every published manifest, operation identity, terminal and protection record, and existing deletion proposal. Any unfinished/resumable writer conservatively blocks all cleanup indefinitely, not just its known object references. Cancel explicitly or resume/finish it first; age is irrelevant.
  2. Compute retained saved states and union their object/member references. Read complete provider inventories; providers without that capability fail closed. Unknown objects lacking protection metadata cannot be garbage-collected. Cancelled, uploaded-but-unverified objects require full downloaded hash and physical-inventory validation before becoming deletion candidates.
  3. Persist/read back an immutable maintenance/<proposal UUID>/proposal.json. It binds the anchor, retention count, inventory generation digest, full expiring manifests, legacy paths/manifests, exact object descriptors, and stable provider node identities. Confirm its exact compact-JSON SHA-256 and persist/read back authorized.json before any destructive call.
  4. Trash/delete only the approved snapshot manifest files, then separately the approved legacy copy folders. Persist each target's *-trashed.json and *-deleted.json receipt. Empty snapshot directories are harmless and remain.
  5. Before each object trash and permanent delete, freshly recompute references from every remaining snapshot and revalidate terminal operations. A live or protected object cannot be removed. Before trashing existing candidate bytes, fully validate compressed hash/size and physical inventory. Never compact or delete a partially live archive.
  6. Persist/read back done.json only after all target phase receipts exist. Unknown, malformed, missing or inconsistent maintenance phases stop mutations.

All receipts bind the proposal digest. Uncertain mutations repeat only the exact persisted identity; no error-message substring is interpreted as proof of absence. Local state loss does not lose the remote proposal, authorization or progress. Completed proposals retain expired manifests solely to validate historical run completion records. These archived manifests do not protect obsolete objects and replaying their old operations cannot republish expired snapshots.

The local provider binds deletion to filesystem device/inode and validates live and trash containment. The Proton adapter binds it to node UID, freshly enumerates trash, and checks JSON per-node success rather than just process exit status. Its destructive path support is deliberately limited to canonical name-based /my-files/... paths: UID-shaped segments and other virtual roots are rejected. It walks from /my-files, checking each listing's child UID/parent UID and the resolved node's UID, parent UID and decrypted name. A lexically contained path is not sufficient deletion authority. This also rejects unreadable ancestry and the CLI's global UID alias resolution outside an apparent parent. Permanent deletion uses /trash/<name>, never the original live path. Duplicate trash names, unreadable trash entries, changed UIDs and unknown responses stop cleanup for exact-node reconciliation; it never guesses or empties the trash. External manual account changes and concurrently active cloned writers remain outside the approved operational coordination model.

Before creating the remote proposal namespace, planning checkpoints the entire proposal locally. If its initial upload fails, a fresh complete inventory may ignore a provably empty unpublished maintenance directory; it has no deletion authority. Any nonempty namespace missing its proposal still blocks mutations. This recovery works after local journal loss and never infers absence from a download error. A lost response after successful publication instead recovers the exact existing proposal and still requires its exact authorization.

estimated_live_member_bytes and estimated_obsolete_member_bytes count unique uncompressed physical-member bytes against retained logical references. They are estimates of logical liveness, not exact reclaimable compressed bytes. Partially live archives retain obsolete members, and a completely obsolete archive is the smallest reclamation unit. Only currently present, identified archives are counted.

On 2026-10-21, the closure check independently parsed all 252 JSON records in the 18 local raw evidence files and reproduced their documented receipt SHA-256:

docs.title: Preserved limits and safeguards
docs.text:
• All selected regular files are hashed; capture is file-by-file, not an atomic application/filesystem snapshot. Changed files are transferred whole.
  • New uploads are fully verified. Daily reuse checks backed by original verification evidence can miss same-sized remote corruption; scheduled full integrity checks and verified restores remain necessary.
  • Each saved state is independently restorable, including legacy history. Shared physical membership remains distinct from logical snapshot membership.
  • Ownership takeover is explicit and manual-offline: the previous writer must be permanently stopped. This is not server-enforced fencing.
  • Safe cleanup requires exact-scope confirmation, retains newest-N saved states across formats, and protects retained/resumable references. Unchanged checks consume no slot. Retained history is never removed to make upload space.
  • The first new-format run uploads a fresh baseline with capacity estimates. Replacing damaged objects for a new state does not repair older snapshots.
  • Partially live archives keep obsolete members; compaction and block-level deduplication remain deferred.

docs.title: Default incremental backups (#62)
docs.text:
Validation status: local correctness, measurement, Standards, and Spec gates passed; accepted for commit. The source now routes fresh normal-worker runs to v4 incremental storage. No installed service, cloud account, package, or deployment has been changed by this work.

The earlier validation report records preparatory measurements and the blockers that existed before this integration. It is not the current implementation status or final delivery evidence.

docs.title: Ownership and upgrade
docs.text:
• A locally created configuration is bound to the machine's stable OS identity and the fixed absolute configuration directory. Writer UUIDs and epochs are persisted before remote initialization; hostnames and editable set names are not writer identity. Namespace IDs for historical non-UUID set IDs are deterministic, so losing local settings cannot create an unrelated replacement namespace.
  • A verified-empty set can be provisioned automatically by a locally bound configuration. A nonempty or foreign repository is never silently adopted.
  • Imported, copied, and old unbound configurations are read-only. For an old pre-ownership configuration, use Offline writer takeover… once to enroll its verified-empty v4 namespace. This is ownership enrollment, not a format opt-in: there is no user-selectable full-upload mode for fresh runs.
  • Before confirming enrollment/takeover, stop the previous writer's processes, schedules, retries, and access permanently. An in-place upgrade must stop the old executable; any subsequent service invocation must use the new writer. The protocol is manual-offline, not a server lease or a fencing guarantee.
  • Existing remote ownership requires an explicit epoch-changing offline takeover. A durable handoff intent makes a lost response retryable. Restoring copied local state does not itself restore write authority.
  • An unfinished legacy copy resumes in its recorded format and exact namespace, after ownership enrollment where needed. Only a fresh run uses the new default.

The first v4 run uploads a fresh baseline and does not reuse legacy payloads. Before publication work, the worker reports selected uncompressed source bytes plus the discovered existing-history payload size (or explicitly unknown size). Compression, manifests, and metadata change actual use; these are estimates, not quota guarantees. No history is removed to make room for the baseline.

docs.title: Saved states, checks, and integrity
docs.text:
All selected regular files are hashed. Intentional skipped links/special nodes do not invalidate readable regular files. Missing roots, inaccessible directories, enumeration failures, and unreadable selected files are not treated as deletions. Execution prunes excluded trees instead of traversing them for preview data. Durable journals are placed outside selected roots. Volatile application queues, locks, and private coordination state are excluded and shown excluded in Preview; the actual settings file remains eligible, so configuration/home selections do not recursively capture a backup's own changing control state.

New/changed regular files are uploaded whole. Renames and deletions reuse unchanged content. An unchanged check publishes no snapshot and consumes no retention slot. Run details distinguish the last successful check from the last saved change and expose integrity and historical-damage information.

New uploads retain full verification and manifest-last publication. Reused objects retain original verification evidence and daily existence/size checks; those lightweight checks can miss same-sized corruption. Scheduled full integrity checking and verified restores remain necessary. Uploading replacement objects for a new state does not repair older snapshots; affected history is reported.

Capture is file-by-file, not an atomic filesystem/application snapshot. Whole-file edits retransmit the whole file. Partially live immutable archives retain obsolete members; compaction and block-level deduplication remain out of scope.

docs.title: Cleanup and mixed history
docs.text:
The normal history browser discovers and verifies both legacy copies and shared snapshots without requiring a local manifest cache. Old non-UUID IDs and legacy computer/set-name namespaces are associated with the configured set before retention planning. A shared snapshot cannot be deleted with the old whole-copy delete action.

Scheduled backups do not authorize their own cleanup. When retention needs work, the UI reports cleanup needs attention. Choose Review incremental cleanup… and review the exact proposed snapshot, legacy-folder, and unreferenced-object identities. Confirmation authorizes only that proposal. A changed scope requires a fresh review.

Cancelling a preview writes a dismissal, not deletion authority. A crashed/closed preview is recovered similarly before the next writer runs. Already-authorized interrupted cleanup resumes only its durable exact scope. Dismissed proposals cannot retire snapshots or authorize deletion. Retained and resumable references still block object deletion, and unreadable history still fails closed.

The newest-N policy counts saved states across old/new formats. Unchanged checks do not evict history. Saved snapshots survive failed cleanup. Ownership, backup, integrity maintenance, and cleanup continue to serialize their mutations.

Build Release and run the repeatable, local-only matrix from disk-backed storage:

The matrix separately compares v3 full uploads and v4 first/unchanged/small-edit runs, full/selective restores, cleanup, and retained-state restore. Profiles are unmodified current-repository source/QML/docs, an explicitly amplified version of that corpus, and deterministic mixed compressible/pseudorandom data. None is a customer workload or a cloud throughput measurement. Generated fixture contents are independently hashed and restored files/counts are checked.

JSON evidence includes provider operation counts/times, transfer bytes, boundary intervals, dedicated local-plan/hash, capture, compression, publication and verification measurements, boundary samples, and event-observed private staging peaks. The observer accounts for regular-file write growth, truncation, removal, and open unlinked writers; provider-boundary synchronization covers kernel copies/reflinks. The successful serial fixtures do not release bytes between a provider copy and that observation. A unit test checks its accounting and a smoke case requires that it never underreport known boundary samples. Provider times overlap phase times and must not be added to them. Staging samples are logical file bytes, not allocated filesystem bytes or a universal process high-water mark. Restore temporary workspaces are disk-backed; destination trees and their final atomic-placement temporary files are outside the reported private workspace scope. Diagnostic observer overhead is included in these local timings. The matrix uses the production 1 GB staging budget and 1,000-file cap, not the unconstrained budgets of the earlier sizing probes.

Profile Enumerate Plan/hash Private capture Compression Verify/receipt interval Publish manifest Provider upload Provider download R 0.0005 0.0073 0.0107 0.0148 0.0291 0.0134 0.0201 0.0383 A 0.0096 1.1872 1.4446 3.0618 2.3491 0.0273 0.0856 0.0745 M 0.0097 1.1421 1.3882 7.6828 3.1344 0.0303 0.2205 0.0778

docs.title: Archive-target decision
docs.text:
Retain the approximately 1 GB uncompressed requested target, together with the existing 1 GB staging budget and 1,000-file limit. This is a measured choice for the normal configuration, not a promise of 1 GB compressed archives:

  • Production constraints already limited the amplified/mixed v4 baseline to three objects at both 256 MB and 1000 MB. Moving to 256 MB saved only about 2.4% of mixed private-peak/selective-transfer bytes in this trace, with no consistent repeat-level timing advantage.
  • A 64 MB target reduced selective-transfer cost substantially, but raised v4 baseline calls from 122 to 230 and objects from three to nine. It did not reduce observed obsolete member bytes in these edit/delete traces.
  • The small unmodified repository used one object at every target. Fixed verification/control overhead dominates there; no target choice made v4 faster than v3 in that local case.

The default therefore prioritizes fewer remote operations while preserving bounded, fully verified capture. Different latency, selection, file-size and change-rate distributions can favor smaller groups; users must not interpret these local fixtures as measured cloud throughput or a universal optimum.

docs.title: Approved ownership change
docs.text:
The user explicitly approved the manual offline handoff model on 2026-10-20 after the installed cli-drive@0.8.0 help and official source showed no remote per-set fencing API. The installed CLI also reports 0.9.0 available; no claim is made that a CLI upgrade supplies a fence. Current upload commands expose conflict choices, not an expected-owner token. The SDK's revision precondition is narrower than repository-wide fencing across upload/trash/delete.

The amended contract requires one owning computer, disabled old writers before handoff, and one shared local coordination directory. Every execution/provisioning operation holds a QLockFile keyed by set UUID, even if paths/configurations differ. Its default location is ~/.config/omacustos/incremental. Supplying a different state directory is for isolated tests/controlled deployments, not a way to run parallel writers. The anchor is downloaded and exactly checked before every remote write. Wrong computer/epoch/origin, stale continuation identity or malformed history stops work. An unfinished remote operation prevents starting a different operation in that set.

These checks cannot remotely fence a stale process between check and mutation. Do not clone an active identity, run on two computers, use two coordination roots, or hand off while the old machine could restart. No expiring remote lock is used. The manual handoff procedure is specified by #56; user-facing takeover tooling is part of #59. Do not edit the anchor as a substitute for disabling the old writer.

docs.title: Advanced CLI use
docs.text:
This is a non-default development/advanced-user seam. Provision a new empty set namespace; do not point it at legacy copy folders. Generate and preserve a computer UUID once and a set UUID once. Generate fresh operation/snapshot UUIDs for each new logical run; retries/resume use the same pair. Use canonical UUIDv4 strings. Keep the request file private and outside the selected sources.

Example request (replace paths, IDs and sources deliberately):

{
  "remote_set_root": "/my-files/backups/sets/10000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001",
  "set_id": "10000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001",
  "computer_id": "20000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001",
  "origin_computer_id": "20000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001",
  "ownership_epoch": 1,
  "operation_id": "50000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001",
  "snapshot_id": "30000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001",
  "staging_directory": "/home/USER/.local/share/omacustos/staging",
  "staging_budget_bytes": 1000000000,
  "archive_target_bytes": 1000000000,
  "batch_file_limit": 1000,
  "sources": [{"source": "/home/USER/project/main.cpp", "restore": "project/main.cpp"}]
}

build/omacustos-incremental --request request.json --initialize --acknowledge-single-writer
build/omacustos-incremental --request request.json --acknowledge-single-writer

sources is an explicit completed selection with stable restore mappings, not directories to recursively expand. Missing files, symlinks, unsafe/colliding mappings or unreadable sources fail. The library also accepts scanner issues, which fail the whole plan. Use the existing scanner's inclusion/exclusion/mapping rules when integrating into the eventual default worker. No local previous manifest is needed: the executor validates all published snapshot manifests and selects the latest by creation time/UUID. A supplied previous snapshot must agree with that discovery.

SIGINT/SIGTERM cooperatively pause and stop owned CLI children; rerun the same request to resume. --cancel durably abandons that operation without deleting its objects. A prepared publication can still be cancelled; an already committed manifest wins a late cancel. An immutable terminal operation is idempotent: rerunning it reports its original completion/check timestamp, not a new check. Generate fresh operation/snapshot IDs for the next check. JSON output exposes saved/unchanged/ paused/cancelled/waiting/retrying/failed, committed manifest path, separate check and saved-change timestamps, issues, damaged object IDs and affected snapshots.

docs.title: Durable continuation protocol
docs.text:
This is a separate payload-format-4 continuation namespace; the copy-scoped BackupContinuation v2/v3 journals are neither migrated nor reinterpreted. Local journals live below <shared-state>/<sha256(exact-set-root)>/<operation-id>; remote recovery uses the following immutable records:

operations/<operation-id>/
  identity.json                 # version 1, payload_format 4, all IDs/root/epoch/time
  reuse-<uuid>.json              # version 1, protected complete archive descriptors
  prepared-<object-id>.json      # version 1, archive descriptor without receipt
  verified-<object-id>.json      # version 1, same descriptor plus original receipt
  publication.json              # exact complete v4 manifest, immutable final intent
  complete.json                 # version 1, saved/unchanged, timestamps and snapshot
  cancelled.json                # version 1, explicit terminal abandonment

Local prepared checkpoints use QSaveFile without direct-write fallback, syncing directory links/renames. Remote preparation is uploaded and read back before its object. Source capture uses the planner's no-follow descriptor walk, bounded reads, stat consistency and exact hash/mode/nanosecond-mtime comparison with the plan. Captured files are private/read-only; gzip level 3 packing rehashes them. Archives are read-only before upload, with new random IDs and complete physical inventories.

The normal working-space bound includes raw captures, conservative tar/gzip output, and a second compressed download for full verification, plus the existing filesystem metadata reserve. Batches obey both byte and file-count limits. One whole oversized file may exceed the soft budget after free-space preflight and an explicit oversized-file checkpoint; no file is split. Multi-member recovery downloads exceeding a lowered budget enter Waiting. Actual quota/write/flush/ checkpoint failures stop without releasing any retention authority.

Objects and control records never use upload replace/rename/new-revision. Proton JSON-mode unresolved conflicts fail; its automatic identical-content skip is accepted only after mandatory verification. Every newly uploaded or merely prepared-but-recovered object is downloaded, checked for compressed size/SHA-256, complete gzip/tar structure and exact full physical membership/size/SHA-256. This uses a validation-only archive reader; v3 extraction's existing strict behavior is unchanged. Current Proton metadata is conservatively not declared a trustworthy SHA-256 authority. A provider can explicitly certify its content-checksum semantics; the local test provider computes current file bytes.

After full verification: remote original-evidence record → readback → local synced verified checkpoint → release staging. Normal source snapshots and compressed output remain through that checkpoint. Pause/failure unwinds private staging as existing backup recovery does; remote protection remains. A prepared descriptor alone never authorizes reuse. Resume inspects exact object IDs and re-verifies prepared uploads, rather than overwriting or trusting their size. Remote verified evidence and complete inventories reconstruct continuation after local journals are lost. Re-scan current selection until the immutable publication intent exists. After that point, recovery finishes that captured state, not newly changed local source bytes.

Daily reuse requires the durable original receipt, fresh existence/content size, and a matching trustworthy checksum where supported. It does not download all reused archives. Size-only checks can miss same-sized corruption until full integrity maintenance or restore. An unchanged successful check creates only a terminal operation/check record, not another snapshot or retention slot.

The executor now runs scheduled full integrity slices before backups and cleanup; --check-integrity explicitly starts/resumes a cycle. The JSON integrity report distinguishes coverage and corruption from daily checks.

For confirmed missing/corrupt reused data, current local files are repacked into fresh objects. Report all saved snapshot IDs referencing each damaged object and preserve their manifests; no historical repair is claimed. Network/authentication, malformed or ambiguous listing/metadata and unreadable history are unknown health, not absence. They stop execution without guessed replacements or cleanup. Conflicting immutable descriptors are corruption and stop work.

docs.title: Publication and cleanup protection
docs.text:
All new verified and reused healthy references must pass before publication intent is prepared, synced locally, uploaded and read back remotely. The complete v4 snapshots/<snapshot-id>/manifest.json is uploaded last. Readback must match the prepared document and schema before durable local success, then remote completion. A lost upload response is reconciled by exact identity/content on resume. Never rewrite a published snapshot or broaden an immutable publication intent. If intent references subsequently damaged data, cancel/start a new operation rather than silently changing what was committed.

All operation/reuse/prepared/verified/publication records protect their object references while unfinished. Pause has no age expiry. Cancel needs a durable marker; a lost cancellation response is retried, not assumed successful. Completed snapshots take over their own live references; terminal leftover objects become candidates only for the separately authorized reference-aware cleanup phase.

The write phase never makes room by deleting history. Local/remote quota exhaustion preserves all old states. A successful saved result can now propose opt-in reference-aware retention, with exact-scope confirmation and the same set UUID mutation lock. Do not point legacy cleanup at sets/<UUID>. Incremental uploads are still not the default worker behavior.

docs.title: Automated coverage
docs.text:
incrementalrepository-test injects interruption at preparation, protection, upload, verification, remote/local checkpoint and publication boundaries. It tests lost responses, remote evidence recovery after local-state loss, current-source changes versus frozen publication, exact subset inventory retention, changed-only uploads, no-download daily checks, the deliberate same-size-corruption limitation, fresh-ID damage replacement and affected history, quota failures, cancel, owner/ epoch changes, local exclusion, protected work and empty states. A complete offline Proton-adapter run uses the CLI filesystem fixture, including noninteractive conflict-failing uploads. No cloud mutation is needed for these tests.

Review-driven regressions also cover an identity upload failing before remote creation with a changed retry/check time (resume and cancel), strict terminal record fields/timestamps/snapshot consistency, and lowered-budget recovery. Reuse matching builds previous logical-reference and recovered-object hash sets once; it does not scan all logical entries for each physical archive member.

Completed cleanup proposals retain expired manifests for validating historical completion records without treating them as live object references. Missing or mismatched history without a validated completed proposal still fails closed.

docs.title: Scheduled integrity and backup health (#61)
docs.text:
Historical component delivery record. Normal workers now advance this protocol too; the UI also offers a full check. See current integration.

The advanced omacustos-incremental executor advances full integrity maintenance before each backup and before starting cleanup. This does not enable incremental backups in the ordinary v3 worker or install a new system schedule. Invoke the advanced executor daily using the same owning installation and shared state path.

docs.title: Schedule, budget and coverage
docs.text:
A missing remote ledger is due immediately; otherwise a cycle starts 30 days after the last successful completion. --check-integrity --request request.json --acknowledge-single-writer starts a cycle immediately or resumes the unfinished one. Each invocation processes one archive at a time, stopping between objects after one hour or 10 GiB of archive downloads. Request settings integrity_time_budget_ms and integrity_byte_budget override those positive soft limits. One archive may exceed the remaining slice. The existing staging budget, free-space checks and single-oversized-file exception remain enforced; the report names oversized single-file objects. Oversized multi-member archives enter Waiting.

Every retained manifest is schema-validated before work. The sorted worklist includes every distinct physical archive referenced by retained snapshots and unfinished operation preparations, verifications, reuse and publication intents. Prepared uploads are included even without an original receipt; missing prepared bytes cannot be certified. Shared objects count once, with their entire physical size/inventory, not just the subset a snapshot uses. Conflicting descriptors stop the check. Completion re-enumerates reachability and verifies known revisions again; new references are included on resume and only proven unreachable objects disappear.

Full verification downloads and checks SHA-256, gzip/tar structure and every physical member. This deliberately also downloads checksum-capable objects on their first check in each cycle, rather than assuming their physical structure. Fresh trustworthy checksums can detect damage before a download. Daily reuse remains original-verification evidence plus existence/size and trustworthy checksums when available. Without a trustworthy checksum, daily checks cannot detect same-sized corruption. Daily checks never refresh original full-verification timestamps.

docs.title: Durable evidence and recovery
docs.text:
Append-only records, separate from deletion proposals:

integrity/<cycle UUID>/plan.json
integrity/<cycle UUID>/checks/<object UUID>/<binding SHA-256>.json
integrity/<cycle UUID>/complete.json
integrity/<cycle UUID>/cancelled.json
integrity-damage/<object UUID>.json

The version-1 plan records owner/epoch, cycle ID, start time and sorted complete physical descriptors. A coverage receipt binds that cycle, exact descriptor, observed content revision/size, method, timestamp and good/damaged result. Each receipt is uploaded immutably and read back before syncing the local cursor. Loss of a local cursor uses remote evidence. Failed receipt uploads are rechecked; a lost upload response is reconciled against the exact persisted receipt. Completed records embed exact final coverage, count, bytes, plan hash, completion time and explicitly reconciled unreachable plan descriptors. Validation requires every planned object to be covered or proven currently unreachable; receipt bindings are recomputed, not just checked for plausible formatting. Malformed or ambiguous evidence fails closed, never resetting the schedule to a false success. Missing ledger restarts full coverage.

Proton's activeRevision.uid supplies content revision identity, not a trustworthy SHA-256. The SDK's NodeEntity/Revision interface defines this field; no node UID or modification timestamp is substituted. The local provider uses its freshly computed content digest as revision identity. Resume freshly inspects revisions before reusing receipts. A changed revision gets a fresh download. Providers supplying neither revision identity nor trustworthy checksum must re-download previous coverage after interruption; the report warns that a larger budget may be required to finish in one invocation. This conservative fallback never treats unknown revisions as unchanged.

SIGINT/SIGTERM pause cooperatively. Resume uses the same unfinished cycle, with current reachability reconciliation. --cancel-integrity cancels coverage without deleting objects; the next invocation starts a fresh cycle. A cancelled cycle is not successful coverage. Backup, maintenance, takeover and cleanup share the set mutation lock and exact owner checks. Offline takeover requires finishing or cancelling an active cycle; stale-epoch continuations cannot resume. Existing authorized deletion transactions must be reconciled before integrity maintenance; new cleanup is blocked by unfinished, damaged or unknown integrity health.

docs.title: Health and repair
docs.text:
Backup JSON reports last_successful_check and last_saved_change separately. integrity contains status, cycle/start, last completion/next due, overdue, current coverage count/bytes, remaining objects, downloaded bytes, damage, affected historical snapshot IDs, errors and cleanup_blocked. last_coverage on a not-due report describes the last completed cycle, not a claim that newly saved objects were in it. cleanup_needs_attention and cleanup issues are separate from backup success. Maintenance failure does not erase backup timestamps or prevent a current-source backup; known damaged objects cannot be reused even by a size-only provider.

Retry transient authentication/network/staging failures with the same request. For corruption, inspect affected snapshots and restore any recoverable files independently. Run a fresh backup operation with current local sources to create replacement new IDs. Old snapshots remain damaged and cleanup remains blocked; replacement uploads do not repair history. There is no automatic compaction, historical-manifest rewrite or archive overwrite. Cancelling/restarting maintenance does not bypass checking those still-retained damaged references.

Confirmed damage is also saved independently of cycles, in the append-only remote integrity-damage ledger and a synced shared local checkpoint. Cancel, budget expiry and failures cannot make a known-corrupt ID reusable. Local evidence retries a failed remote damage publication; unreadable damage knowledge forbids backup reuse. The blacklist is not cleared by writing a new revision under an old ID.

docs.title: Read-only incremental planner (#57)
docs.text:
Historical component delivery record. Its rollout-status statements are superseded by the default-worker integration.

IncrementalPlanner::plan in native/src/incrementalplanner.{h,cpp} implements source capture and deterministic comparison against exactly one previous v4 snapshot. It is deliberately not wired into today's full-backup worker or UI: the repository contract still gates default rollout on restore, GC and release validation. #58 adds a separate executor using the explicitly approved operational single-writer/manual-offline-handoff model, not remote fencing.

docs.title: Inputs and capture
docs.text:
Supply the stable set UUID, a completed scanner's selected regular files with their stable relative restore mappings, and its scan issues. Any scan issue fails the whole plan: a missing/unreadable source root must not masquerade as intentional selection removal. Existing scanner inclusion/exclusion and collision mapping remain the caller's responsibility. Empty sources with no scan issues explicitly represent an empty selection. Supply the full previous manifest and its selected snapshot ID, or neither for the first baseline. A missing/corrupt expected manifest is an error, not permission to silently start another baseline. Legacy copies are not content-reuse inputs; the first v4 baseline is fresh.

The planner uses the v4 validator with the requested set/snapshot before looking up any content. It rejects unsafe/duplicate restore destinations and file/parent conflicts before opening sources. Absolute source paths must be clean. Linux openat walks every path component with O_NOFOLLOW, so neither parent nor leaf symlinks are followed. Only regular files are read. Nonblocking opens avoid waiting on a source replaced by a FIFO.

Every selected file is read and SHA-256 hashed, even if its size and nanosecond mtime match the previous snapshot. Reads use a 64 KiB chunk, one open file at a time; no whole-file buffer, temporary payload, remote operation, configuration write or staging disk allocation occurs. Metadata still scales with file count. The bounded hash pass applies equally to files larger than the staging budget.

Capture records descriptor identity, size, mode, nanosecond mtime and ctime before reading. After hashing it rechecks both that descriptor and a freshly no-follow opened source pathname, requiring matching device/inode, size, full mode, mtime, ctime and observed byte count. Read errors, content/metadata changes, pathname replacement, unsupported size/mtime range or cancellation fail transactionally: no partial files, removals or archive requirements are returned, and the previous successful-check time is preserved. Each file has its own capture instant; this does not promise a filesystem-wide point-in-time snapshot or protection against a malicious filesystem falsifying stat/hash observations.

docs.title: Deterministic result
docs.text:
files are sorted by case-sensitive restore path, and each has a disjoint logical change classification:

  • Added: destination absent from the previous logical state (including rename destinations and newly selected files).
  • Changed: existing destination with different size/SHA-256, permission bits 0777, or nanosecond mtime.
  • Reused: destination, bytes and supported restore metadata unchanged.

Content reuse is independent of that classification. Every matching (size, SHA-256) from the previous snapshot's logical entries can supply an archive and member, including for an Added rename/duplicate or Changed metadata-only file. Choose the lowest (archive ID, member) tuple, independent of manifest or scan order. Multiple files can reference that same content. Do not search an archive's obsolete physical members, other snapshots, local history, or other sets. New duplicate content not present in the previous snapshot remains whole-file upload work; this planner does not introduce within-run payload packing/deduplication.

requiresUpload() is true only without a reusable archive/member. Upload candidates are whole new/changed file contents, never unchanged archive neighbors. removed lists old destinations absent from the new selection, sorted independently. requiredArchives contains exactly the reused archive descriptors sorted by ID, preserving complete physical inventories and original verification evidence, including members no longer logically referenced. New object IDs and packing are the later uploader's responsibility.

snapshotRequired is false only with a previous snapshot whose complete logical state (paths, content and supported metadata) is unchanged. An initial empty baseline requires a snapshot; a later empty-to-empty check does not. Removing the last file requires a saved empty state. Physical reference choice alone is not a logical change and does not create another snapshot.

docs.title: Successful checks, saved changes and later execution
docs.text:
The request supplies checkedAt and the prior lastSuccessfulCheck. Reject an invalid or regressing check time. Successful local planning returns that check time separately from lastSavedChange (the previous manifest's creation time, invalid before the first saved state). A changed plan does not advance last saved change: only verified publication can do that. Both fields are exposed in the result so a later worker/UI can distinguish checks from saved states.

For an unchanged plan, the future writer must still perform the contract's remote reuse health checks, then durably record the successful check without creating a manifest or consuming retention. The planner itself writes no check history and does not claim current remote integrity or authorize cleanup. Its successful-check timestamp is a candidate local observation, not an end-to-end backup success until those later checks pass. Existing full-backup UI timestamps remain unchanged.

Because the planner keeps no staged payloads, a later executor must not upload directly from these source pathnames. Recapture each upload candidate into the existing private, bounded staging workspace, check captured size/hash/mode/mtime against the plan, and replan on mismatch. Preserve immutable staged bytes through packing/upload/verification/checkpoint release, as required by the repository contract. A successful local plan does not relax staging capacity, original verification evidence, fresh reuse health checks, source-change checks or manifest publication ordering. This seam cannot authorize the later remote operations.

docs.text: incrementalplanner-test uses real local files and nanosecond metadata, covering baseline/unchanged and empty states, additions/edits/removals, selection changes, renames/duplicate content, deterministic matching/ordering, metadata-only changes, same-size/same-mtime edits, physical-only inventory members, same-set validation, unsafe mappings, scan failure, symlinks, missing files, in-read writes/truncation/ pathname replacement and cancellation. Race tests mutate sources at the planner's cooperative read checkpoints, without sleeps or cloud calls.

docs.title: Incremental repository contract (v4)
docs.text:
Rollout-status statements below record this component's original delivery point. Current default-worker integration and validation are documented in the #62 delivery report. The protocol's integrity, ownership, restore, and deletion requirements remain in force.

Status: normative design for #56, not enabled in the default worker. Changed-file incremental backups replace full uploads only after the release gates below pass. The pure IncrementalManifest::validate boundary implements the manifest schema; it performs no network I/O and does not authorize publication, restore, or deletion. The separate v4 restore adapter validates remote identity and physical inventories. Existing v1/v2/v3 readers, exact v3 membership checks, and full uploads are unchanged.

Ownership amendment for #58 (2026-10-20, explicitly approved by the user): the CLI-backed implementation uses one operational writer with manual offline handoff, not server-enforced fencing. This supersedes the original fencing requirement; it does not relax payload verification, restore validation or deletion safeguards. See executor and recovery details.

docs.title: Scope and trust
docs.text:
Target documents and source code. Changed files are saved in full, in bounded tar.gz archives (gzip level 3). Capture is file-by-file, not filesystem-wide or application-consistent. No block deduplication, cross-set sharing, compaction, historical archive migration, or live database/VM consistency is promised.

Trust the authenticated account, TLS/CLI transport, and the owning implementation to report verification honestly. SHA-256 protects against accidental corruption, not a malicious account writer replacing both data and manifests. A receipt is durable evidence of an observation, not a signature or a fresh remote check. Untrusted downloaded JSON, paths, and archives always require validation. External account tools can bypass coordination: concurrent manual edits/deletion are outside the safety model and must be warned against. Integrity checks detect such damage; they cannot make an account administrator obey the protocol.

docs.title: Stable identity and namespace
docs.text:
Generate cryptographically random UUIDv4 identifiers: one computer_id persisted outside editable hostnames, one set_id at set creation, and fresh object, snapshot, and operation IDs. Lowercase canonical UUID text is mandatory. Export/import on another installation never grants write ownership. Cloning a computer identity requires explicit recovery, not automatic scheduling. Renaming computer/set labels does not move storage or alter identity. Losing local identity makes discovery read-only until takeover. Preserve the original computer ID across ownership changes.

<chosen-remote-root>/sets/<set_id>/
  repository.json
  objects/<object_id>.tar.gz
  snapshots/<snapshot_id>/manifest.json
  operations/<operation_id>/...       # durable protection and recovery records
  maintenance/...                     # integrity coverage and deletion intents

repository.json is a version-1 control record: application: "omacustos", set_id, immutable origin_computer_id, current owner_computer_id, positive ownership_epoch, and coordination: "manual-offline-v1". Human-readable labels are kept outside this minimal authorization record. Provision it using a fresh, empty namespace with conflict-failing upload and verified readback; never adopt an existing conflicting ID. Anchor updates require confirmed offline handoff, not a claimed conditional remote write. Display labels are never authorization. The root is chosen explicitly during remote-only recovery; discover repositories below its direct sets child, not by guessing hostnames. Legacy discovery remains separate.

All mutation paths must be constructed below the exact validated set root from typed IDs; manifests cannot supply an absolute remote path. Reject root aliases, parent traversal, separators in IDs, mismatched set/snapshot selections, and provider node identities whose resolved parent is outside that root. A set root, objects root, or snapshots root is never a deletion target.

docs.title: Manifest schema
docs.text:
Examples: baseline and later shared subset. These are metadata-only illustrative fixtures, not downloadable archives; hashes and compressed size are placeholders. The latter deletes b and renames a, but embeds the complete original archive inventory. Neither requires the other manifest.

Every object below has exactly the listed keys (no silent extensions). Arrays must have the indicated types. Reject unsupported versions rather than falling back to v3. Numbers are JSON integers in 0..2^53-1 unless narrowed below; hashes are 64 lowercase hex SHA-256 characters. Timestamps use valid UTC YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ. JSON object keys must be unique at the producer; Qt's JSON parser resolves duplicate keys before schema validation, so do not use raw JSON byte equivalence or duplicate-key interpretation as an authorization signal.

Object Required fields and constraints Manifest version: 4, application: "omacustos", set_id, origin_computer_id, owner_computer_id, ownership_epoch (positive), snapshot_id, created_at, status: "complete", archives array, entries array Archive id (object UUID), remote (exactly objects/<id>.tar.gz), size (positive compressed bytes), sha256 (compressed bytes), members (nonempty complete inventory), original_verification Physical member path (safe relative tar name), size (uncompressed bytes), sha256 (file bytes) Original verification method (download-sha256 or remote-sha256), verified_at, sha256 (must equal archive digest); embedded in the archive descriptor, binding its ID, size, complete inventory and digest Logical entry restore (safe relative destination), archive (object UUID), member (physical path), size, sha256 (both exactly match physical member), mode (integer 0..511, POSIX permission bits), mtime_ns (canonical unsigned decimal string, 0..9223372036854775807)

All IDs use the UUIDv4 representation above. Set/snapshot IDs must match the selected remote location; original computer identity must match the repository anchor. Old snapshots may have an earlier owner/epoch; this does not prevent restore. The pure validator checks schema and selected set/snapshot, not the remote anchor. Archive IDs and physical names per archive are unique. Every archive must have at least one logical reference, but not every physical member need be referenced. Multiple destinations may reference the same physical member (identical files). Destinations are unique; both physical and destination sets reject file/parent-file conflicts. Empty entries plus empty archives represent a complete empty saved state.

Relative paths reject empty components, ., .., leading/trailing /, backslash, NUL, ASCII controls and DEL. Names are case-sensitive and not Unicode-normalized. On filesystems with incompatible name equivalence, fail on collisions before placement, never merge/overwrite silently. Sources and local configuration are not required in the manifest. A complete manifest is the whole logical saved state, never a delta, ancestor pointer, or list of just changed files. Source failure prevents a v4 complete publication; preserve resumable work and older snapshots, report the failure, and do not run retention. Legacy incomplete copies stay readable.

docs.title: Restore metadata and validation
docs.text:
Support regular file bytes, relative destination, POSIX mode bits 0777 and mtime in nanoseconds since Unix epoch (nonnegative signed-64-bit range). Compare all of these for unchanged-state detection; a metadata-only change creates a new manifest but may reuse content. Hash every selected local file; size/mtime is no substitute. Reuse from the immediately previous complete snapshot by size/SHA-256, including renames; no search through arbitrary historical snapshots yet. Deterministically choose the lowest object-ID/member tuple when several matches exist.

Do not preserve owners/groups, ACLs, xattrs, sparse allocation, birth/ctime, directory metadata or empty directories, symlinks, special files, hardlink identity, setuid/setgid/sticky bits. Explain these limits in the restore UI. Files are staged privately, then mode/mtime applied to the verified temporary file before atomic placement. Unsupported metadata or precision loss is reported, not silently claimed as exact restoration. Recheck destination symlinks before commit; no direct write fallback. Already committed files retain existing partial-restore semantics.

For every downloaded archive, check compressed size/hash, complete gzip stream, CRC/trailer and tar termination. Validate all physical members, including unselected ones, against the full inventory (names, size and SHA-256). Reject extra, duplicate, missing, unsafe, nonregular or linked tar members. Do not materialize unselected members. Tar permission/time fields are not restore authority: use logical metadata, so reused content can have different mode/mtime. Never adapt the v3 extractor by merely allowing unexpected members. The v4 restore adapter explicitly passes the physical inventory and logical selection separately.

docs.title: Ownership and operational coordination
docs.text:
Serialize backup, full integrity maintenance, retention, and recovery mutations per set. Read-only discovery/restore need no write ownership. Local process/file locks remain useful but are insufficient across computers or cloned configurations.

The installed Proton CLI 0.8.0 and inspected upstream commands do not expose per-set fencing tokens or caller-supplied conditional writes/deletes. The SDK's CurrentRevisionID on revision creation is not a per-set mutation fence. The CLI's local events PID lock is not cross-computer coordination. Do not pretend an advisory remote lock file or an expiring timestamp provides these guarantees.

Approved supported model: exactly one owning computer and one shared local coordination-state directory per set. Backup, integrity maintenance and cleanup must all hold its non-expiring process lock (keyed by stable set UUID), and re-read the exact owner/epoch anchor before remote mutations. Reject mismatches. Never schedule writes from restored/imported configurations on another computer, and do not clone a writer identity into active use. No remote lease is acquired or stolen. Unfinished operations remain protected indefinitely, regardless of their age.

Explicit limitation: a second computer, a second coordination-state directory, or an already-running old process can bypass local exclusion. Owner rechecks are diagnostics, not atomic fencing; a stale writer can race the next remote call. This model relies on the operator disabling the old writer before handoff. There is no safe online/automatic takeover through the CLI. Strict stale-writer rejection would require an enforcing service or future provider capabilities.

Manual offline handoff must show the exact root/current owner/epoch and require: disable old schedules/services and auto-retries; stop all GUI/CLI writers and wait for transfers to exit; prevent the old installation from later restarting (revoke its access or remove/disable its writer configuration); reconcile or explicitly abandon protected operations/intents; then assign a fresh computer ID and increment the ownership epoch, upload/read back the anchor, and enable only the new writer. If the old machine cannot be secured against resuming, remain read-only. A local journal cannot resume under a changed epoch. Never infer abandonment from time. User-facing offline takeover tooling is documented in recovery.

Payload/control creation uses fresh immutable IDs and conflict-failing JSON-mode uploads, with mandatory readback verification. Never use replace/rename/new-revision for objects or manifests. The CLI may skip identical content; verification must still prove the expected bytes. Final snapshot discovery validates a complete v4 manifest; missing, draft, malformed or conflicting content is not restorable.

docs.title: Verification evidence and health policy
docs.text:
1. Before upload, journal an immutable object descriptor and inventory to synced, atomic local state, and persist a verified remote operation protection record.
  2. Upload exclusively to a fresh ID. Fully verify compressed size and SHA-256 against private staged bytes. A trustworthy provider checksum must describe the current plaintext content revision, not encrypted storage size, ETag, upload-request echo, user metadata, or a different revision. Otherwise download and hash; quota/staging shortage enters Waiting, not size-only success.
  3. Only then persist original_verification locally and remotely in that operation record, read/hash it back, sync local verified checkpoint, then release staging. Copy the descriptor and original receipt unchanged into every referencing manifest. Thus loss of local state does not lose the evidence. Conflicting descriptors/receipts for one immutable ID are corruption: stop and investigate.
  4. On every daily reuse/check, require that evidence and matching identity; fetch fresh existence and plaintext size plus trustworthy SHA-256 if available. Do not refresh verified_at based on size. Missing evidence requires a new full verification and durable receipt before reuse. Authentication/network/ambiguous listing errors are unknown health, not absence: stop/retry, no cleanup.

Without trustworthy remote hashes, daily checks can miss same-sized corruption until a full check or restore. Display “Existence/size checked; full integrity last checked ; next due ”, never “all bytes verified today”. Local hashing does not prove remote health. Restore always hashes downloaded bytes independently. Confirmed damage creates a fresh replacement object from current local bytes when possible, never overwrites an ID. Report every historical snapshot affected; a new successful backup does not repair old manifests or authorize deleting damaged history.

docs.title: Scheduled full integrity maintenance
docs.text:
Begin a full cycle at least every 30 days since the last completed cycle, and on explicit Check integrity. Loss of the remote coverage ledger makes it due now. Coverage is every live shared object reachable from all retained snapshots and protected operations, not just the newest copy. Validate every retained manifest first. Each object gets current revision size/hash verification; download/hash when trustworthy SHA-256 is unavailable, then validate its full physical inventory as for restore. Even with a remote checksum, physical structure must have been validated at original creation; a changed revision requires downloaded validation.

Capture a sorted (object ID, size, digest, inventory) worklist under coordination. Use the existing configured staging disk/budget and one archive at a time, with the existing explicitly reported single-oversized-file exception. Default run budget: 1 hour or 10 GiB downloaded, stopping between archives (one archive can exceed the soft budget). Resume next daily worker invocation before cleanup; show coverage count/bytes, last completion, remaining work and overdue status. Never mark a cycle complete merely because its budget expired. Do not starve maintenance behind repeated backups: once due, advance its slice before the next backup.

After each verified object, atomically persist remote coverage (cycle ID, expected descriptor, checked revision, method and timestamp) and sync the local cursor. Crash resumes the first uncommitted object; an uncertain commit is rechecked. Pause preserves the worklist; cancellation/lost ledger restarts coverage, not a false success. Before completion, reconcile reachability: add newly live objects unless full verification since cycle start already covers them, drop only proven unreachable ones. Bind evidence to revisions; unknown/changing revisions require rechecking. Completion records its exact coverage and timestamp remotely. Maintenance failures preserve history, expose affected snapshots, and block automatic GC until resolved. These are logical budgets, not a claim of bounded network-call duration.

docs.title: Manifest-last publication and interruption
docs.text:
An operation protection record (version 1) contains set/operation/snapshot IDs, owner/epoch, all prepared and reused object descriptors, verification states and publication intent. The v4 executor records these as immutable per-object records and reuse-protection batches below the operation, not a repeatedly rewritten whole-history document. Re-scan current selected sources until publication intent fixes the final logical selection. Persist and verify protection under local exclusion before uploading or claiming any object. Extend it durably before each new object; local journals alone never protect remote reachability. Never overwrite published objects/manifests. Unknown upload results are reconciled by exact ID and hash; conflicting bytes cause a new ID, never replacement.

Ordering: prepared local journal → remote protection → upload → full verification → remote receipt → synced verified local checkpoint → release staging → daily reuse checks → validate complete manifest → conflict-failing manifest upload last → download/hash/schema/location verification → durable run success → operation completion → retention eligibility. Manifest bytes must be assembled before upload; the provider must not expose a partial file at its final name. A successful unchanged check records last successful check remotely in the operation history without publishing a snapshot or consuming retention; retain last saved-change time.

Discovery lists only direct snapshot IDs, then reads manifest.json. Missing file means unpublished; malformed file is visible as damaged, never restorable or cleanup authority. A valid complete manifest at its final path is the commit point; a lost upload response does not make it unpublished. Remote-only discovery needs no run history. Invalid or unknown-version snapshots block cleanup, rather than being silently ignored. The app must not advertise success until readback succeeds.

Interruption Recovery under operational single-writer coordination Before remote protection No upload permitted; discard/rebuild local preparation After protection, before/within upload Protect named objects; inspect exact names; retry missing objects, fully hash existing objects before accepting them After upload, before receipt/checkpoint Reverify; prepared state is not verification evidence After receipt, before staging release Validate receipt/identity and current reuse health; checkpoint before release Before manifest Resume same snapshot/operation; rescan current sources, reconcile refs, and update protection before changing objects Manifest upload or readback outcome unknown Read exact path; identical valid bytes mean committed; absent means retry; conflicting/invalid bytes mean quarantine and stop After manifest, before local success Recover committed snapshot and success without uploading a duplicate; cleanup remains gated on durable success Pause/cancel/owner loss Pause retains protection indefinitely; cancel durably records abandonment under local exclusion; never infer abandonment from time alone. An already committed manifest wins a late cancel

Protection is retired only after a verified committed snapshot takes over its references, or explicit abandonment by the current owner with old writers disabled. Lost/unreadable operation state blocks GC. Reinstall recovery enumerates remote operations before resuming; it never treats local journal absence as abandonment.

docs.title: Retention, deletion authorization, and recovery
docs.text:
Keep configurable newest-N successful saved states across positively identified legacy copies and v4 snapshots, sorted by creation time then snapshot/copy identity. Unchanged checks consume no slot. Preserve incomplete/damaged/unknown states unless separately and explicitly authorized for removal; they never evict good history. Upload the fresh baseline without referencing legacy archives. Check capacity and warn about coexistence with old full history; insufficient capacity stops the run, never deletes retained history to make room.

Only a durably successful, verified publication can initiate automatic retention. Hold shared local exclusion throughout planning and mutations, with all other computers' writers disabled. Read all manifests, protection records, unresolved maintenance/deletion intents, and repository anchor freshly. Any unreadable, ambiguous, malformed, foreign or unsupported record stops GC. Do not use a possibly incomplete listing: provider must guarantee complete enumeration or a revision-consistent inventory. No age-only orphan collection.

Persist/readback a deletion intent (version 1): proposal UUID, set/owner/epoch, exact snapshot paths and manifest hashes, legacy copy paths/identities, exact object IDs/paths/digests/sizes, reachability generation, confirmation and per-target phases. First cleanup requires exact-scope user confirmation, matching current proposal bytes; changed scope requires fresh confirmation. Later cleanup uses the saved policy but still durably records each exact scope before mutations. Existing local cleanup locks and run coordination remain required. They do not provide remote fencing; the operational single-writer assumption applies to cleanup too.

Order: authorize intent → remove only approved snapshot manifests/copy folders → persist each result → freshly recompute retained/protected reachability → trash only whole unreferenced objects → persist phase → recheck reachability immediately before permanent deletion → persist completion. No object may be trashed while a retained or published-not-yet-removed snapshot, resumable operation or unresolved intent protects it. The current intent's deletion candidates are not themselves live references; other unresolved intents are protection until reconciled. New writers cannot reuse objects already in a trash/delete intent; finish/reconcile it first. Never delete partially live archives or guess compressed reclaim from member sizes. Track logical live/obsolete bytes only as estimates.

Snapshot deletion first ensures a crash leaves extra objects, not dangling retained references. After an uncertain trash/delete response, inspect exact identity and trash state, then idempotently resume the persisted phase; never broaden targets or replace an unfinished proposal. New epoch takeover revalidates every target and requires renewed authorization. A transient failure stops the phase, retains intent and reports retryable cleanup attention. Backup success remains success: “Backup saved; cleanup needs attention”. No empty-trash command or deletion of other sets. Legacy folder deletion retains existing containment/identity checks and never authorizes deleting shared objects. Integrity errors cannot authorize retention.

docs.title: Shared-archive recovery (#59)
docs.text:
Historical component delivery record. Default workers now use the same v4 storage/restore protocol; see current integration.

The advanced build/omacustos-incremental entry point discovers/restores v4 snapshots with only an authenticated Proton CLI and a selected remote root. No local settings, sources, schedules or journals are required. Default worker rollout and shared-object cleanup remain gated on #60 and release validation. BackupManifest still reads only v1–v3; IncrementalRestore is the separate v4 schema/location/anchor adapter used by BackupCatalog::verifyCopy.

build/omacustos-incremental --discover /my-files/Backups
build/omacustos-incremental \
  --snapshot /my-files/Backups/sets/SET_UUID/snapshots/SNAPSHOT_UUID \
  --destination "$HOME/Recovered"
# Repeat --select for multiple exact logical paths; omit it for all files.
build/omacustos-incremental \
  --snapshot /my-files/Backups/sets/SET_UUID/snapshots/SNAPSHOT_UUID \
  --destination "$HOME/Recovered" --select documents/report.txt

Discovery reads only direct UUID repositories below sets and direct UUID snapshots. Missing manifests are unpublished; malformed/foreign manifests appear damaged with no restorable files. Missing or metadata-mismatched archives make their logical files unavailable. Discovery metadata is not full byte verification. Restore downloads each needed archive once and checks compressed size/SHA-256, complete gzip/tar structure and every physical member's name, regular-file type, size and SHA-256, including obsolete/unselected members. Extra, duplicate, linked and unsafe members are rejected. Only selected files are materialized. No ancestor manifests are read.

Restore preserves bytes, relative destination, POSIX mode bits 0777 and nanosecond mtime. It does not preserve owners/groups, ACLs, xattrs, links, sparse allocation, special files, directory metadata or empty directories. Use a fresh destination to reproduce a saved file list: unrelated existing files are not deleted. Mode/time are applied and verified on the atomic temporary file before placement; unsupported precision fails explicitly. Symlink containment checks and disabled direct-write fallback remain in force. Already committed files remain placed if a later file fails (existing partial-restore behavior).

docs.title: Replacement computer / offline ownership handoff
docs.text:
Discovery/restore does not grant writes. There is no server-enforced fencing or safe online takeover in the installed CLI. The approved #58 manual model applies:

  1. Inspect the exact repository.json root, owner and epoch.
  2. Stop the old writer, schedules/services, transfers and retries.
  3. Prevent restart by disabling/removing old writer configuration or revoking its access. If this cannot be secured, remain read-only.
  4. Reconcile/cancel unfinished operations under the old owner first. Handoff refuses unfinished/conflicting operations and maintenance records. Neither age nor lost local journals authorizes abandonment or deletion.
  5. Prepare a request identifying the current set, origin, owner and epoch, fresh operation/snapshot UUIDs and shared disk-backed state/staging directories per execution. sources may be omitted for takeover. Generate a fresh replacement computer UUID; do not clone the old identity.
build/omacustos-incremental --request current-owner.json \
  --takeover NEW_COMPUTER_UUID --acknowledge-single-writer \
  --confirm-old-writer-disabled

Handoff holds the shared local mutation lock, rereads the exact old anchor, checks protected operations, durably checkpoints before/after intent, updates only the mutable anchor and verifies fresh readback. Origin stays unchanged; epoch increments. Unknown/conflicting updates require read-only inspection, not blind repetition. No schedules are recreated/enabled, no journals migrate epochs and no archives, snapshots or protection records are deleted. Explicitly update the new writer request before enabling it. Old identity requests fail owner checks; these checks are not an atomic server fence and do not replace operator isolation of the old installation.

docs.text: Confirmed with the user on 2026-10-20. These decisions do not certify release readiness or authorize cloud access or deployment.

docs.title: Cleanup authorization
docs.text: Scheduled backups must not automatically confirm their own cleanup proposals. The worker saves the backup and reports cleanup needs attention. A user-facing preview must present the exact deletion proposal for explicit confirmation before the reference-aware executor deletes anything. If the proposal changes, obtain fresh confirmation; do not substitute a general newest-N policy authorization.

docs.title: Writer provisioning
docs.text:
Only a verified-empty remote set may be provisioned automatically. Bind its stable writer UUID to the local installation, not an editable hostname or display name. Imported or copied configurations remain read-only for discovery and restore until explicit offline takeover confirms the previous writer is permanently disabled. Missing local state must never silently authorize adopting existing remote history or creating a replacement writer over it.

These policies are now implemented and covered by worker/controller failure tests. See current integration and delivery evidence.

docs.title: Source enumeration prerequisite
docs.text:
Directory open/read errors must be distinguishable from successful enumeration of an empty directory. The scanner now exposes BackupPreview::scanErrors; both existing backup execution paths refuse publication when this list is nonempty. The preview UI includes these paths among skipped paths. Errors while browsing explicitly excluded directories for preview do not invalidate the selected files.

scanerrors-test injects both directory-open failure and a directory-read error after a real entry has been delivered. It checks that neither legacy nor bounded archive execution publishes a manifest, even if other selected files are readable. It also checks normal hidden-file enumeration and excluded-directory behavior. Real permission-denial cases additionally cover selected roots and descendants without read or directory-search permission, across all three execution modes. Those cases require an unprivileged test process.

The incremental selection adapter now carries enumeration errors, missing roots, and unreadable selected paths into IncrementalPlanRequest::scanIssues. Intentionally skipped links/special nodes remain outside regular-file selection. An incomplete scan cannot authorize removals. The scanner-only results below remain historical preparation, not the final rollout evidence.

docs.title: Reproducible local benchmark
docs.text:
Build the real core implementation with Release optimizations:

cmake -S native -B /tmp/opencode/omacustos-62-release -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build /tmp/opencode/omacustos-62-release --target incremental-benchmark -j 4

From a writable disk-backed working directory, run:

/tmp/opencode/omacustos-62-release/incremental-benchmark 1073741824 4096 64000000 documents-code
/tmp/opencode/omacustos-62-release/incremental-benchmark 1073741824 4096 256000000 documents-code
/tmp/opencode/omacustos-62-release/incremental-benchmark 1073741824 4096 1000000000 documents-code

Repeat with mixed for deterministic half-code/half-pseudorandom file content. Arguments are selected bytes, file count, uncompressed archive target, and profile. Fixtures are synthetic, not a representative customer corpus. Seeds and source generation are fixed; identities/timestamps vary. Each invocation creates and removes its own private local fixture, and requires eight times the selected bytes free as a conservative fixture capacity check. It never uses Proton or a configured backup root. Compression stays tar.gz with the production defaults. The fixture uses a staging budget of at least four times the archive target and raises the file-count limit to the fixture file count, so those constraints do not silently cap the sizing comparison. This is not a measurement of the normal 1 GB staging budget or 1,000-file group limit.

JSON lines record these scenarios separately:

  • Fresh v4 baseline; unchanged check; small edit plus rename and deletion.
  • Full restore of both old and new states after hiding local coordination state.
  • Single-file restore of an unchanged file from its original archive, rather than the small new archive containing the edited file. Select the middle logical path to avoid biasing the result toward a short final archive.
  • Exact-proposal preview/confirmation and cleanup down to one saved state.
  • Full restore of the retained state after cleanup.

Independent SHA-256 fixtures and exact output file counts check every restore. An unchanged check must publish no manifest and upload no objects. Renames and deletions must not retransmit unchanged payloads: only the edited file is packed. Cleanup must require confirmation, perform no deletion during preview, and leave exactly the intended newest snapshot. Two tiny CTest smoke cases cover both fixture profiles; timings are never gates.

docs.title: Measurement boundaries
docs.text:
• Total scenario time excludes fixture generation, independent expected hashes, and post-restore comparison. Restore time includes discovery/verification and placement. Cleanup includes proposal, confirmed execution, and readback discovery.
  • boundary_intervals_ns sums time since the preceding durable checkpoint into the named ending boundary. planned/capturing includes scan/hash work. Preparation/capture and compression span preparing, prepared-sources, and prepared-local: packing also emits control polls, so these cannot isolate compression CPU time. uploaded and object-verified include transfer/verification and ordering overhead. Repeated boundary names accumulate. These are not exclusive CPU subphase measurements.
  • Provider operation counts and nanoseconds measure individual local calls; they overlap boundary/wall times and must not be added to them. Uploaded and downloaded bytes count successful local transfers, including control metadata. They do not measure failed partial transfers or network wire overhead.
  • The provider withholds checksums to exercise download/hash verification, but delegates metadata inspection to LocalProvider, which hashes internally. Consequently even unchanged runs include extra local reads. No CLI startup, encryption, network latency, rate limiting, or real quota behavior is measured.
  • checkpoint_sampled_writer_staging_peak_bytes is a lower-bound sample at checkpoints and provider boundaries, not an exact high-water mark. It excludes restore staging, source/restore trees, and independent member extraction space. Frequent capturing/preparing control polls do not walk staging; doing so would add quadratic measurement overhead as the file group grows.
  • Inventory records distinguish compressed referenced archive bytes from total physical/obsolete uncompressed member bytes in the newest snapshot. Obsolete member bytes are not reclaimable compressed bytes, nor necessarily obsolete across retained history. Shared archives are not compacted.
  • These probes do not compare to fresh v3 full backups, isolate scan/hash from journal overhead, or provide authorized-cloud or large-corpus evidence.

docs.title: Remaining release blockers
docs.text:
1. Integrate stable local computer identity and repository ownership with normal backup-set creation, worker scheduling, queue pause/cancel/resume, and recovery. Imported/restored configurations must remain read-only until explicit takeover; never silently initialize a new writer over existing history.
  2. Scan the configured roots/inclusions/exclusions into complete source mappings; preserve scan failure as a failure, not a deletion. Preserve the durable format of interrupted legacy copies rather than converting them during resume.
  3. Surface first-baseline capacity estimates/warnings (old history plus new baseline), distinct successful-check/saved-change/integrity status, cleanup attention, and mixed-format history in normal worker/UI paths.
  4. Integrate newest-N retention with exact deletion authorization. The advanced executor requires explicit per-proposal confirmation; do not bypass that safety protocol just to make scheduled cleanup automatic.
  5. Add worker/GUI end-to-end failure-injection tests for these integration paths. Existing advanced-executor tests alone do not prove the default upgrade path.
  6. Gather representative sizing evidence, including v3 comparison, repeats, larger corpora where practical, and accurate staging/subphase instrumentation. Select the production target only from sufficient evidence. The current approximately 1 GB target remains unchanged; that is not a measured selection or a performance promise.

Whole-file edits require whole-file retransmission. Capture is non-atomic, file-by-file, not an application-consistent filesystem snapshot. Lightweight existence/size reuse checks may miss same-size corruption until a scheduled full integrity check or restore. A partially live archive retains obsolete members. No benchmark authorizes weakening verification, retained-history protection, publication ordering, exact-scope deletion, or offline ownership handoff.
